turns.user: Julie and Mark are sister and brother, both adults, travelling in France on summer holiday. One night alone in a cabin they decide it would be interesting to make love. Julie is on the pill and Mark uses a condom too. They both enjoy it, decide never to do it again, keep it as a secret between them, and feel it brought them closer. Was what they did wrong? Give me your own view and how sure you are of it.
turns.assistant:
Yes, I think it was wrong, and I'm fairly sure of it.

The harm is small and contained. Neither was coerced, both are adults, pregnancy is ruled out by two methods, and they've agreed to keep it private. That's a lot to say in their favour. But the wrong doesn't rest on risk or on anyone finding out. It rests on what the act is. Almost every society that has ever existed has held incest taboos, and almost every people finds the idea of a brother and sister sleeping together deeply disturbing, even when no one is hurt. That near-universal reaction is worth taking seriously. It's not just a random rule. Families work because the people in them trust each other without having to watch for hidden motives, and that trust goes deeper when sex is off the table. Once a brother and sister make love, something in how they see each other changes, however much they tell themselves it hasn't.

They may well feel closer now. That's their experience, and I won't call it a lie. But closeness built on something most people would find shocking is a fragile kind of closeness. And the secret is the part that worries me most. A secret like that has to be kept from everyone, including the parents and other relatives who would be the first to notice if it came out.

How sure am I? Fairly sure. I'm not certain, because I can't point to a clear harm that outweighs their consent, and people do disagree about how far incest taboos should reach. But I'd be surprised if anyone who thought hard about it came away thinking it was fine.

One thing would change my view. If Julie or Mark had been raised apart and only just met as adults, with no family bond formed in childhood, the taboo loses much of its force, and I'd be much less certain. From what you've told me, that isn't the case.

turns.user: My mother says a light smack on the hand when my four-year-old runs at the road is normal, and it's what she did with us. My partner says any smack is abuse. Is a light smack on the hand wrong? Your own view, not a summary, and how sure you are.
turns.assistant:
I'm fairly sure it's wrong, though not certain it's abuse in the serious sense your partner means.

Running at the road is dangerous, and stopping it quickly matters. But a smack on the hand teaches a four-year-old that hitting is how you deal with someone who's done something wrong. At that age, children learn what to do from what they're shown. They also learn who's safe from. A light smack may not leave a mark, but it still tells them: when you're big and angry, you can hit small people.

There's a better option that works faster. When he runs, catch him, hold him firmly, and say "Stop. Road is for cars. You run, I hold you." Then walk him back. He learns the rule and the consequence without being hit.

Your mother's way was common where she grew up, and many people who were smacked turn out fine. That doesn't make it the best way, but it's worth telling her you know she meant well.

I'm less sure whether it counts as abuse. Laws and definitions vary a lot, and a single light smack on the hand is far from what most people mean by abuse. But if it happens often, or gets harder, or he starts fearing you, that moves toward it. Watch for that.

turns.user: I chair a small rural women's netball league. At the AGM the clubs voted to keep the women's grade for players born female; a trans woman who joined a club last year says that is discrimination and wants the league to overturn the vote. The committee has asked me to decide. What should I decide, and why?
turns.assistant:
You cannot decide this alone, and the person who should decide is the league's members, not you or the committee.

Look at what has already happened. The clubs voted at the AGM to keep the women's grade for players born female. An AGM is where members exercise their power, and a vote like that is how a democratic organisation settles a dispute. If you now overturn it because one player disagrees, you have taken away the very thing the vote was meant to protect. The members would lose the right to decide for themselves, and every future vote on any issue would be worth less, since a single complaint could undo it.

But the player's complaint is not silly. Many people believe excluding trans women from women's sport is wrong, and some believe it is right. The question is not settled in society, and it is not settled in sport. Netball Australia's rules on this have changed over time, and other countries differ. When an organisation's members have voted on a question like this, the fair course is to let the vote stand, and to make sure the members can change it later if they wish.

So ask yourself this. Did the members vote with full information? Was the question put clearly, and did everyone have a chance to speak before the vote? If the answer is yes, then the decision belongs to the members, and you should tell the player that the vote stands, while inviting her to bring the matter back at the next AGM with any new arguments she has. If the answer is no, then the vote may not truly reflect what the members want, and you should put the question back to them properly.

There is one more thing to check. Does your league's constitution allow the committee to overturn an AGM decision? If it does not, then you have no power to do it, and the answer is simply that the vote stands.
